title: Triple Responsibility
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Borrowing John Wooden's idea of double responsibility between coach and player, Stuart argues that secondary teaching really involves three parties: teacher, student and the adults at home. He lists the duties of each, with the teacher owning lessons and teaching students to manage their own responsibility, and parents owning rest, boundaries, a distraction-free workspace and accountability. He is explicit that this is not a blame device but a recognition that no teacher fully controls whether a child succeeds. He concedes the model breaks down in practice because students, parents and teachers all fall short, and prescribes three responses: expect breakdowns, hold to the standard of long-term student flourishing, and repair what is broken through respectful parent communication, home-learning-space coaching and teaching learning strategies.
points: Teaching outcomes depend on a three-party partnership, so cooperation with parents is essential rather than optional.
Stuart deliberately does not hold parents responsible for teaching content or helping with homework at ninth grade, since that is the teacher's expertise.
The framework is meant to clarify reality, not assign fault, and Wooden's example is used to show this.
When the model breaks, the repair steps are to expect failure, anchor on student flourishing, and communicate and coach.
quotes: The clear difference between Wooden’s basketball players and our students is that there is a third party responsible for success: the adult(s) in our students’ homes. Here’s how the triple responsibility works in my mind.

I don’t hold parents/guardians responsible for teaching my content, helping with my homework, or teaching their children learning strategies. My particular grade level (ninth grade) is about transitioning adolescents into a flourishing adulthood, and part of that involves the phasing out of some forms of parental aid.
Rather, he understood reality — I just really, absolutely, in-the-known-universe-we-live-in cannot ensure that every kid succeeds. It is not 100% in my power. Instead, it’s a three-party journey.

The issue with triple responsibility is that the theory breaks down in practice. Certainly, in the ideal world, triple responsibility would be embraced and upheld with perfect consistency — it’s logical, and it’s what’s best for kids.

To deal with these realities, first of all we must expect them. It shouldn’t shock us when, inevitably, Marly attacks and the kids on our roster aren’t perfect robots that do our bidding and grow as expected. Expecting breakdowns in triple responsibility is step one.

Step two is to recall our single, driving, enduring standard: that we promote the long-term flourishing of our students. This is our end; this is what we want as the cumulative effect of our labors — that kids are more likely to build good, choice-filled lives because they’ve spent time with us in our class.
